text:
Predicates:
ScheduleMeeting(x, y) ::: x schedules a meeting with y.
Employee(x) ::: x is an employee.
Customer(x, y) ::: x is a customer of y.
GoToCompany(x) ::: x goes to the company building today.
Lunch(x, y) ::: x has lunch in location y.
InCompany(x) ::: x has lunch in the company building.
AtHome(x) ::: x has lunch at home.
WorkRemotely(x) ::: x works remotely from home.
InOtherCountry(x) ::: x works in another country.
Manager(x) ::: x is a manager.
WillAppearInCompany(x) ::: x will appear in the company today.
Premises:
∀x (ScheduleMeeting(x, y) → Employee(x)) ::: Anyone who schedules a meeting with a customer is an employee.
∀x (Employee(x) → (∃y Customer(y) ∧ ScheduleMeeting(x, y))) ::: Everyone who has lunch in the company building or at home, and works in the company, schedules meetings with customers.
Employee(x) ∧ (InCompany(x) ∨ AtHome(x)) → (Lunch(x, inCompany) ∨ Lunch(x, atHome)) ::: Employees have lunch either in the company building or at home.
AtHome(x) → WorkRemotely(x) ::: If an employee has lunch at home, they are working remotely from home.
InOtherCountry(x) → WorkRemotely(x) ::: All employees who are in other countries work remotely from home.
¬Manager(x) → ¬WorkRemotely(x) ::: No managers work remotely from home.
WillAppearInCompany(x) ↔ Manager(x) ::: James will appear in the company if and only if he is a manager.
Conclusion:
(Manager(james) ∨ InOtherCountry(james)) → ¬(AtHome(james) ∨ WorkRemotely(james)) ::: If James is either a manager or in other countries, then he does not have lunch at home or work remotely from home.
(AtHome(james) ∨ WorkRemotely(james)) → ¬Manager(james) ∧ ¬InOtherCountry(james) ::: If James has lunch at home or works remotely from home, then he is neither a manager nor in other countries.
